entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Heaven (Tiantan) is a 15th-century Chinese imperial sacrificial complex in Beijing, where the emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties performed elaborate annual rituals to pray for good harvests and communicate with Heaven. A UNESCO World Heritage site since 1998, it is considered the most important example of traditional Chinese ceremonial architecture and embodies the ancient Chinese cosmological belief in the emperor as the 'Son of Heaven' mediating between earth and the divine.

Construction began in 1406-1420 CE under the Yongle Emperor, who also built the Forbidden City. The complex covers 2.73 square kilometers — four times larger than the Forbidden City — and contains three primary structures: the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests (Qiniandian), a triple-gabled circular hall on a three-tiered marble terrace; the Imperial Vault of Heaven; and the Circular Mound Altar. The complex was designed to embody Heaven (circular) and Earth (square) in its geometry.

The winter solstice ritual was the most important ceremony in the imperial calendar: the emperor would proceed to the altar, declare himself before Heaven, and offer sacrifices of silk, jade, and animals. The acoustics of the Echo Wall — a circular wall surrounding the Imperial Vault — allow whispers to travel 65 meters along the curved surface, a feature likely intentional for ritual communication. After the collapse of imperial rule in 1912, the Temple of Heaven was opened to the public by President Yuan Shikai.
